name: Sensor calibration fingerprint (SensorID)
plain: Per-device factory calibration in accelerometer and gyro data identifies a phone with no ID API.
meaning: Factory calibration error is unique per unit. SensorID read about 42 bits on an iPhone 6S, survives resets and uninstalls, and also hit some Pixel phones.

android.api_surface: Raw accelerometer or gyroscope reads, then statistical analysis
android.note: Pixel 2 and Pixel 3 shown vulnerable in the paper

ios.api_surface: iPhone 6S and others vulnerable through iOS 12.1; Apple added noise to sensor data in iOS 12.2

limits.headline: Can maybe recognize your phone from tiny sensor flaws, with no ID or prompt
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when an app or page collects motion sensor data
can: Collect motion data and study factory calibration errors that differ by phone
Use the pattern to tell phones apart without a device ID
Recognize the same phone across apps and sites in a research setting
cannot: Work reliably on all phones; the research named specific models
Work on iPhone after Apple added noise to sensor data (iOS 12.2 and newer)
Use Safari motion data on iPhone without the permission
See what you do, only who the phone seems to be
limits.reach_label: A hidden ID that follows the phone
limits.differs: Research showed iPhone 6S and some Pixel models vulnerable. Apple added noise after iOS 12.1.

story.what_it_is: Tiny factory flaws in your phone's motion sensors can act like a fingerprint that identifies it.
story.for_you: You never see or feel it. Every phone's motion chips are slightly off in their own way. That quirk stays the same after a reset or deleting apps, so a tracker could recognise your phone again.
story.for_makers: Researchers showed it works with no ID and no permission, so it is attractive to trackers who lost other IDs. Honest makers do not need it. Platforms respond by rounding the data or limiting how fast sensors can be read.

use_cases.example: An ad kit reads the sensor quirks and recognises the same phone across two different apps with no advertising ID.
A fraud tool uses a sensor fingerprint to catch one person running hundreds of fake accounts on one device.
A game studio could spot a banned cheater who reinstalled on the same phone, though few do this.
An analytics SDK tries to stitch visits from the same phone after the user turned off tracking.
A retailer ties a sale browsing session to a phone that cleared its cookies.
A research team shows the attack on iPhone 6S and some Pixel phones, which led Apple to add noise.

story.android_note: Some Pixel models were affected, and Android caps sensor speed without a special permission.
story.ios_note: Apple added random noise to the calibration data after the research about iPhone 6S and 7 phones.

abuse: Persistent cross-app ID that survives reset

history.change: Apple added noise to sensor data after SensorID report
